name: Mesopotamian
earliest_record: Gilgamesh poems, about 2100 BCE; Enuma Elish, about 1100 BCE
summary: The city-states of Sumer, Akkad and Babylon told of gods who built the world from a defeated sea, and of a king who searched for a way to escape death.

name: Egyptian
earliest_record: Pyramid Texts, about 2400 BCE
summary: Egyptian tradition imagined a world rising from dark waters, sustained by the sun god's daily journey and by the promise of order over chaos.

name: Canaanite
earliest_record: Ugarit tablets, about 1400–1200 BCE
summary: Stories from the coastal cities of the Levant follow the storm god Baal, the sea and death, and the cycles of fertility and drought.

name: Hittite / Hurrian
earliest_record: Hittite cuneiform tablets
summary: The Hittite court preserved Hurrian songs and myths, including the storm god Teshub and the vanishing god Telipinu.

name: Persian / Zoroastrian
earliest_record: Avesta; Shahnameh, about 1010 CE
summary: Zoroastrian sacred tradition sets truth against the lie, while the Shahnameh turns ancient heroic legend into a national epic.

name: Minoan / Mycenaean
earliest_record: Linear B tablets; later Greek retellings
summary: Aegean palace cultures left tantalising traces of bull rituals, labyrinthine buildings and gods whose names survive in later Greek scripts.

name: Greek
earliest_record: Homer and Hesiod, about 800–700 BCE
summary: Greek poets gave the Mediterranean a family of gods on Mount Olympos and a store of heroic adventures that later cultures never stopped retelling.

name: Etruscan
earliest_record: Inscriptions, mirrors and tomb art
summary: Etruscan religion read the will of the gods in lightning and the livers of sacrificed animals, and passed much of its divination to Rome.

name: Roman
earliest_record: Virgil and Ovid, 1st century BCE–1st century CE
summary: Rome adopted Greek gods under new names and added its own founding legend of Aeneas, Romulus and the destiny of the city.

name: Celtic
earliest_record: Irish texts, 8th–12th centuries CE; the Mabinogion
summary: Irish and Welsh storytellers preserved tales of the Tuatha Dé Danann, heroic champions and voyages to the Otherworld.

name: Norse
earliest_record: Poetic and Prose Eddas, 13th century CE
summary: Norse tradition imagined nine worlds held in a great ash tree, gods who knew they would one day fall, and heroes who faced that ending with courage.

name: Slavic
period_text: pre-Christian to about the 10th century CE and later folklore
earliest_record: Late chronicles and folklore collections
summary: Fragments in chronicles and centuries of folklore remember a storm god, a underworld god and spirits of house, forest and river.

name: Baltic
period_text: pre-Christian to about the 14th century CE
earliest_record: Chronicles and folk songs
summary: Baltic traditions kept a sky god, a thunder god and a rich world of household and nature spirits alive in song long after conversion.

name: Finnic / Sámi
earliest_record: Kalevala, compiled 1835, from older oral poems
summary: Singers of the north told of a world made by a creator god, of the forging of the Sampo, and of shamans who travelled between worlds.

name: Caucasian (Nart)
period_text: ancient oral tradition; Nart sagas collected in the 19th century
earliest_record: Nart sagas, recorded from the 19th century
summary: Peoples of the Caucasus share the Nart sagas, where a race of heroes battles giants and brings fire and culture to the world.

name: Hindu
earliest_record: Rigveda, about 1500–1200 BCE; Ramayana and Mahabharata, later
summary: A living family of traditions, with many gods and goddesses, epic heroes, and stories that are still sung, performed and debated today.

name: Buddhist narratives
earliest_record: Jataka tales, preserved in later collections
summary: Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's previous lives, often as an animal, and teach generosity, patience and insight through story.

name: Chinese
earliest_record: Shang oracle bones, c. 1250 BCE; Shan Hai Jing; Journey to the West, 16th century CE
summary: Chinese tradition weaves Shang divination, Daoist cosmology, Buddhist pilgrimage and local cults into stories of creator giants, immortal queens, dragon kings and the rebel Monkey King.

name: Japanese
earliest_record: Kojiki, 712 CE; Nihon Shoki, 720 CE
summary: Shinto tradition tells of kami who made the islands, of the sun goddess Amaterasu, and of a world kept in balance through offerings and purification.

name: Korean
earliest_record: Samguk Yusa, about 1280s CE
summary: Korean legends tell of a bear and a tiger who wished to become human, of the founder Dangun, and of household gods and shamans.

name: Tibetan / Bon
earliest_record: Bon and Buddhist texts, later written down
summary: Tibetan sacred traditions blend Bon and Buddhist cosmology, with mountain deities, sky beings and elaborate stories of liberation.

name: Mongolic & Turkic
earliest_record: Epics such as Manas and Dede Korkut, written down later
summary: Peoples of the steppe honoured Tengri, the eternal blue sky, and passed down long heroic epics about Manas, Alpamysh and other champions.

name: Southeast Asian
earliest_record: Inscriptions, chronicles and oral epics
summary: The region's traditions weave local spirits and ancestors with Hindu and Buddhist epics, from the Ramayana of Java to the naga legends of the Mekong.

name: Siberian / Arctic
earliest_record: Oral traditions recorded from the 19th century
summary: Arctic and Siberian peoples tell of a creator or sky being, of the raven and the loon, and of shamans who journey to other worlds.

name: Yoruba / Orisha
earliest_record: Oral Ifá tradition; written records from the 19th century
summary: Yoruba sacred tradition tells of Olodumare and the orisha, including Ọ̀rúnmìlà, Obatala, Ogun and Èṣù, and of the divination system Ifá.

name: Akan / West African
earliest_record: Oral tradition; Anansi stories are widely shared
summary: Akan storytellers made Anansi the spider a clever trickster whose small size and quick wit turn the tables on stronger creatures.

name: Dogon & Mande
earliest_record: Oral tradition; the Sundiata epic, written down later
summary: Mande bards keep the epic of Sundiata, founder of Mali, while Dogon traditions describe star beings and the ordering of the world.

name: Bantu
earliest_record: Oral traditions of many kingdoms and peoples
summary: Across central and southern Africa, Bantu-speaking peoples tell of creator gods, culture heroes and spirits who inhabit land, water and sky.

name: Maya
earliest_record: Popol Vuh, written in the 16th century
summary: Maya tradition tells of the Hero Twins who defeat the lords of the underworld, and of the several attempts to make human beings from mud, wood and maize.

name: Aztec / Mesoamerican
period_text: Olmec from about 1200 BCE; Aztec 14th–16th centuries CE
earliest_record: Colonial-era codices and chronicles
summary: Aztec narratives describe a world created and destroyed in cycles, the sun god Huitzilopochtli, and the journey of the dead to Mictlan.

name: Andean
earliest_record: Colonial chronicles recording earlier oral traditions
summary: Inka and earlier Andean traditions honour the sun Inti, the earth mother Pachamama, and the mountain lords who guard the highlands.

name: North American Indigenous
period_text: ancient oral traditions, recorded from the 17th century onward
earliest_record: Oral traditions of many distinct nations
summary: Hundreds of distinct Indigenous nations keep their own sacred stories and histories; this game lists the category only, and does not speak for any nation.

name: Amazonian & Caribbean
earliest_record: Oral traditions; colonial-era records
summary: Amazonian and Caribbean peoples tell of creator beings, animal ancestors and spirits of river and forest, in many distinct traditions.

name: Polynesian
period_text: far Polynesia settled about 1000–1300 CE; older roots
earliest_record: Oral traditions recorded from the 19th century
summary: Māori, Hawaiian and other Polynesian traditions tell of sky and earth parents, of Māui who fished up islands, and of voyages across the great ocean.

name: Aboriginal Australian
period_text: more than 60,000 years of continuing tradition
earliest_record: Oral tradition, song and art
summary: Aboriginal Australian traditions hold the Dreaming as a continuing creative order; stories belong to specific peoples and countries and carry law and ceremony.
